name: Tokyo Arts and Space
overview: Contemporary art centre of the Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture, with an exhibition venue, TOKAS Hongo, at 2-4-16 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, and an artist residency, TOKAS Residency, at 2-14-7 Tatekawa, Sumida-ku (Artsticker, Internet Museum).

Established in 2001 as Tokyo Wonder Site, an initiative for supporting young artists, and renamed Tokyo Arts and Space in 2017 (ASEF culture360, Artsticker). Japanese Wikipedia says the project started on Governor Shintaro Ishihara's initiative and opened in 2001 as Tokyo Wonder Site Hongo.
The Creator-in-Residence Program launched in 2006 and moved to the Sumida site in 2014 (Artsticker).
funding_verdict: Tokyo Arts and Space: run by the Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture, whose parent body is the Tokyo Metropolitan Government (Japanese Wikipedia)
wider_context: Assembly, 2006: in the fourth regular session of 2006, Japanese Communist Party member Nobuo Yoshida told the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly that Tokyo Wonder Site was run as a personal project of the governor's family, citing Ishihara's fourth son, the painter Nobuhiro Ishihara, and the appointment of Imamura and his wife as director and deputy director. The Culture Bureau director-general answered that no remuneration had been paid to Nobuhiro Ishihara for a stage backdrop, that public spending on him was about 600,000 yen in travel costs, and that 830,000 yen in adviser fees had been paid to the account of Kayoko Iemura, whom it had commissioned as a facility adviser in 2001. Yoshida had said that 730,000 yen reached the account of Imamura's wife in March 2002, before her formal appointment. Ishihara answered that he would correct and apologise if any spending were illegal, and called the line of questioning "a poor way of thinking, typical of the Communist Party" (Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly net report; translation).

J-CAST News, 12 December 2006: reported that the Tokyo government paid about 550,000 yen for Nobuhiro Ishihara's travel on a 2003 Europe research trip for Tokyo Wonder Site, and that about 1.2 million yen of public money paid to a performer covered a January 2004 trip to paint a backdrop. It quotes Ishihara at a 24 November 2006 press conference: "If someone irreplaceable were needed, I'd use anyone" (translation).
Japanese Wikipedia states that Imamura, a Tokyo government adviser, and his wife took the director and deputy director posts through their acquaintance with Ishihara.
This concerns the programme as it ran under its earlier name, Tokyo Wonder Site, which the governor started and the Tokyo government funded and controlled.

name: Watari-um
overview: Private contemporary art museum in Jingumae, Shibuya, near Gaienmae Station on the Ginza Line (Time Out, Art Space Tokyo).

Founded by Shizuko Watari and opened in September 1990. It grew out of the commercial Galerie Watari, which she directed from 1972 to 1989 (Wikipedia, Art iT). In 2012 she co-wrote a book on its activities with her children Koichi Watari and Etsuko Watari (Art iT). Koichi Watari is the museum's representative (Bijutsu Techo).
The name "Watari-um" joins the family name Watari with "museum" (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Watari-um: privately run: admission income, a 2020 crowdfunding campaign and corporate support

name: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM)
overview: Media art centre in Yamaguchi City, Yamaguchi Prefecture, on the south side of Yamaguchi City Central Park, about 20 minutes' walk from Yamaguchi Station (Wikipedia).

Opened on 1 November 2003, after a planning process that began in the late 1980s and a construction pause in 2002 (YCAM history). Run under the Yamaguchi City Foundation for Cultural Promotion (YCAM annual report FY2021).
Directors: Toru Yamamoto became General Director in 2005, Akeo Adachi Director in 2007, Hajime Masuda in 2018, Tadayuki Miwa in 2020, Motoo Isobe in 2022, and Masuda returned in 2024 (YCAM history).
funding_verdict: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media: public: Yamaguchi City pays most of the programme budget, with Agency for Cultural Affairs grants

name: Yokohama Museum of Art
overview: Municipal art museum at 3-4-1 Minatomirai, Nishi-ku, in the Minato Mirai 21 district of Yokohama, next to the Yokohama Landmark Tower (museum website, Wikipedia).
Opened on 3 November 1989 under a Yokohama city ordinance, first as a facility of the Yokohama Exposition (museum annual report FY2024).
Building by Kenzo Tange: a facade 180 metres wide, with granite among its exterior cladding, and the central Grand Gallery (museum website, annual report).
funding_verdict: Yokohama Museum of Art: mainly public: the City of Yokohama pays the operator, the Yokohama Arts Foundation, a management fee

name: Makan Art Space
overview: Independent, artist-run contemporary art space at 21 Nadim Al-Mallah Street, Jabal Al-Weibdeh, Amman (Fillip, Spring 2012; TransArtists).

Founded by Ola Khalidi (Ola El-Khalidi), who opened it in April 2003 as an alternative space for young artists free of restrictions. Before launching she worked at the Amman cultural café Blue Fig and the NGO Beirut DC and spent about eight months researching the project (Bidoun, Summer 2004).
Khalidi said she did not want to call it a "gallery": its purpose was to develop young artists by hosting projects and building connections (Bidoun, 2004).
funding_verdict: Makan Art Space: self-funded at the start, later supported by grants: founder's own money first, then a 2008 AFAC-backed programme and other grants

name: A. Kasteyev State Museum of Arts
overview: National art museum in the Koktem-3 microdistrict of Almaty (22/1), now styled the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Art Museum after being granted national status.

Opened on 16 September 1976 from the collections of the Shevchenko Kazakh State Gallery (founded 1935) and a museum of decorative and applied art (founded 1970). Renamed in 1984 after the Kazakh artist Abilkhan Kasteev (1904 to 1973) (Wikipedia).
Named for Abilkhan Kasteev, a Kazakh painter (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: A. Kasteyev State Museum of Arts: public: Kazakhstan's Ministry of Culture and Information
wider_context: Noise dispute: Tengrinews reported on 14 July 2021 that the museum had been fined 230 MRP (about 670,000 tenge) over air-conditioner noise that residents of the Central Esentai Residence next door complained about, and ordered to fix the problem within 30 days. The museum says the housing complex was built illegally inside its protective zone. The Ministry says it never approved the construction and that the cooling system is needed to keep storage at 18 degrees Celsius plus or minus 1 under a 2015 order. The museum and the developer then negotiated.

Unverified: an unnamed former director took about 1.544 million tenge from the museum, through a freight refund from a 2007 exhibition transport contract and a refund on a demolition job, from Express-K citing Almaty's financial police, reported by Vesti.kz on 13 March 2009. The article reports only the start of the trial and no verdict; no later reporting was found.

name: National Museum of the Republic of Kazakhstan
overview: State history and culture museum at Tauelsizdik Avenue 54, Astana (museum website).
Built in 2014 and designed by architect Vladimir Laptev. The design began with "the idea of a waving flag" (Wikipedia, citing QazaqCulture).
The building has seven blocks of one to nine storeys in blue glass and white marble, with about 14,000 square metres of exhibition space across 11 halls (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: National Museum of the Republic of Kazakhstan: state budget: Kazakh Ministry of Culture and Sports
wider_context: Vladimir Potanin, whose collection supplied the show, was sanctioned by the UK on 29 June 2022 under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019, with a full asset freeze (UK government). The same page reports the UK Charity Commission opened an inquiry into The Potanin Foundation that day.
Wikipedia lists sanctions on Potanin from the United States (15 December 2022) and Canada (6 April 2022).

The connection to the museum: the museum's news item of 1 August 2026 says the 140 objects come from Vladimir Potanin's collection and lists the "V. Potanin Olympic Collection" project among the organisers of the exhibition, which runs until 30 September 2026.

name: Gapar Aitiev Kyrgyz National Museum of Fine Arts
overview: National art museum on Sovietskaya Street, across from the opera house and near Ala-Too Square in central Bishkek (SRAS Museum Studies Abroad).

Grew from a picture gallery the Kyrgyz regional Communist Party committee opened in 1934 (Voices on Central Asia); it opened on 1 January 1935 with 72 Russian works from the Tretyakov Gallery and the Russian education commissariat, chosen by its founder, the painter Semyon Chuikov (museum site).
It became a state museum in 1944 and a national museum in 1998 (director Mira Dzhangaracheva to 24.kg, 2019).
funding_verdict: Gapar Aitiev Museum: public: Kyrgyzstan's culture ministry
wider_context: The first Feminnale of contemporary art, 56 artists from 22 countries, opened at the museum on 28 November 2019 (Human Rights Watch; New East Digital Archive). Culture Minister Azamat Zhamankulov met its opponents and ordered works he called "provocative" and "amoral" removed (Human Rights Watch); six pieces went, Falkova's "Evermust" among them (New East Digital Archive), and a performance by Julie Savery involving nudity was cancelled (ArtReview).
On 2 December the minister set up a commission to study the show (24.kg); on 5 December MP Kurmankul Zulushev called for a police investigation (Human Rights Watch).

Director Mira Dzhangaracheva left after threats against her and her staff, including to "tear me apart, to rape me"; the government opened an investigation into the threats on 6 December 2019 (Human Rights Watch). She said she stepped down voluntarily; 24.kg reported the minister removed her. A protester from the nationalist group Kyrk Choro called the show pornographic (New East Digital Archive).
In June 2019 her predecessor, Yuristanbek Shygaev, asked to leave after media reported he had returned two originals from storage damaged (24.kg).
In August 2021 the painter Taalaibek Usubaliev said there was talk of removing his painting of six presidents from a show at the museum, with no direct order (24.kg).
These cases took place at the museum, under the ministry that funds it.

press_items.title: Taylor Dafoe, "Kyrgyzstan Censored a Feminist Art Show at the National Museum of Fine Arts. Now Its Director Has Resigned" (2019)
Hillary Margolis, "Feminist Art Exhibit Threatened in Kyrgyzstan" (2019)

name: Arete Foundation for Arts and Culture
overview: Libyan non-profit arts organisation in Tripoli, founded in 2012, a few months after the 2011 revolution (Arab Fund for Arts and Culture, AFAC). Newsweek calls it an NGO.
Founded by the poet Khaled Mattawa and his wife, the artist Reem Gibriel (MERIP interview, 17 Nov 2021). They moved to Tripoli in January 2012 (Hisham Matar in Newsweek).

Named for Arete of Cyrene, a Greek-Libyan philosopher (University of Michigan LSA, 17 Sep 2014). Newsweek gives the name's meaning as knowledge, excellence in work, or living up to one's highest human potential.
funding_verdict: Arete Foundation for Arts and Culture: grant-funded: Arab and European arts funds, local businesses and the Libyan Ministry of Culture, as named by its founder

name: Zolak
overview: Belarusian community-run venue, "ZOLAK Micro Art Residence", on the third floor at Vytenio g. 50D, Vilnius, entered through the former ELFA factory grounds at Panerių g. 37 (stated by Zolak).

Reform.news reported on 11 June 2025 that the space would open on 14 June 2025, and named its creators as the activist Piotr Markielau, the writer Alina Nahornaja and the photographer Siarhei Hudzilin. Zolak's footer credits Markielau.

Reform.news puts the space at about 150 m2, with an event space, coworking area, rest zone, kitchen and a sauna. Zolak lists a gallery of 39.14 m2, a crypto bar of 21.36 m2, a coworking and meeting room, a kitchen and shower, and guest rooms for up to 8 people.
funding_verdict: Zolak: privately funded: private contributions, a residency subscription, space rentals and event donations; does not plan to take grants

name: Musée National du Mali
overview: National museum in Bamako, on Avenue de la Liberté (Artes Sere).
Opened on 14 February 1953 as the Musée soudanais, attached to the Institut français d'Afrique noire. It became the Musée national du Mali at independence in 1960 (Wikipedia, French).
On 8 March 1982 it moved into new premises in stabilised earth ("banco stabilisé"). Architect Jean-Loup Pivin drew on traditional architecture (Wikipedia, French).
funding_verdict: Musée National du Mali: public: the Malian state, with foreign project grants

name: Rencontres de Bamako
overview: Biennale of contemporary African photography and video held in Bamako, Mali, since 1994 and also called Bamako Encounters and the African Biennale of Photography (Biennial Foundation).

Organised by Mali's Ministry of Culture and co-produced with the Institut français. Exhibitions are spread across Bamako in museums, galleries, foundations, art centres, public venues and French cultural centres (Biennial Foundation).

The Musée national du Mali was the main venue of the 14th edition, held from 16 November 2024 to 16 January 2025 under the theme "Kouma", the spoken word, with Morocco as guest of honour (Le360 Afrique, Diemba Moussa Konaté, 18 November 2024).
funding_verdict: Rencontres de Bamako: organised by Mali's Ministry of Culture and co-produced by the Institut français, with Royal Air Maroc as a long-standing partner

press_items.title: Christian Kravagna, "Bamako 2007: On the seventh Rencontres africaines de la photographie" (2008)

name: Museo Experimental El Eco
overview: University museum of art, architecture and design on James Sullivan street in the colonia San Rafael, Mexico City (Crónica, 6 August 2025).

Designed by Mathias Goeritz at the invitation of Daniel Mont and opened in 1953 (Crónica). The Gaceta UNAM article (Roberto Frías, 9 October 2025) says Mont commissioned it and Goeritz conceived it as an inhabitable sculpture ("escultura habitable").

In its first years it showed works by Henry Moore and Carlos Mérida and presented dance and music. After Mont's early death the building was used as a restaurant, cabaret and theatre, then occupied by the Centro Universitario de Teatro and CLETA, and lay unused for years (Crónica).
funding_verdict: Museo Experimental El Eco: mainly public: UNAM, a public university funded by the federal government

name: Museo Universitario del Chopo
overview: Contemporary art museum of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) at Dr. Enrique González Martínez 10 in Santa María la Ribera (Gaceta UNAM), under UNAM's Coordinación de Difusión Cultural (Spanish Wikipedia).

The building is a prefabricated Jugendstil structure of iron and glass, designed by Bruno Möhring as a machine hall for the Gutehoffnungshütte works and shown at the 1902 Düsseldorf exhibition; the businessman José Landero y Coss bought it and shipped it to Mexico, where Ludwig Bacmeister assembled it (Chilango, Sara De Lille, 17 February 2023; Gaceta UNAM, 2025).

It opened in 1913 with a Japanese exhibition, then housed the natural history museum until that museum moved to Chapultepec in 1964, leaving the building empty (Chilango, 2023). UNAM's director general of cultural outreach from 1973 had it restored with the approval of Rector Guillermo Soberón (Gaceta UNAM, 2025).
funding_verdict: Museo Universitario del Chopo: mainly public: UNAM, itself funded by the federal government

name: Colección FEMSA
overview: Corporate art collection of the Mexican company FEMSA, based in Monterrey, focused on modern and contemporary Latin American art with an emphasis on Mexican work (CIMAM).
It began in 1977, when the founding family of FEMSA donated "El maizal (Milpa seca)" by Gerardo Murillo (Dr. Atl) (CIMAM).

Its history is tied to the Museo de Monterrey (1977 to 2000). After the museum phase ended the collection became itinerant, working through loans and collaborations with museums (FEMSA press release, 8 December 2025).
funding_verdict: Colección FEMSA: corporate: part of FEMSA (Fomento Económico Mexicano)
wider_context: SIPAZ, "Chiapas: Protest to cancel Femsa-Coca Cola concession in San Cristobal de las Casas" (posted by the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre on 11 April 2017): on 10 April 2017 organisations and neighbourhoods of San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, marched to demand that the concession of Femsa Coca-Cola be cancelled or its water extraction capped; protesters said the plant extracts more than 750,000 litres of water a day.

Al Jazeera, Peter Yeung, "'Forgotten': How one Mexican city struggles against big industry for water" (8 January 2025): the Femsa-run bottling plant in San Cristóbal has permits to extract more than 300,000 gallons of water a day from the basin of the Huitepec volcano, and a 2017 report by a coalition of environmental and civil rights groups says Femsa pays 2,600 pesos for each water permit in Mexico. Coca-Cola Mexico's spokesperson, Daniela Puerta, said "We always abide by local laws and regulations."
The collection is part of FEMSA, which indirectly owns 47.2% of Coca-Cola FEMSA. The protest and the article name FEMSA and its bottler, not the collection.

name: Museo de los Pintores Oaxaqueños
overview: State art museum (MUPO) at Avenida Independencia 607, at the corner of García Vigil, in the historic centre of Oaxaca de Juárez (Excélsior; Spanish Wikipedia).
Opening dates differ: the Spanish Wikipedia infobox says 2003 and its text 2004; Excélsior (2025) says the museum has run since 2006.

The building opened on 26 January 1686 as the Colegio de las Doncellas de Nuestra Señora de la Presentación, a girls' school paid for by Juan Gómez de Tapia, a priest of Tututepec, and the Portuguese philanthropist Miguel Fernández Fiallo (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo de los Pintores Oaxaqueños: public: Oaxaca state government

name: Fundación Casa Wabi
overview: Non-profit civil association that connects contemporary art with 14 local communities on the Oaxacan coast through programmes based in Puerto Escondido. It also runs Casa Wabi Sabino in Mexico City and Casa Nano in Tokyo (Casa Wabi).

Founded by the Mexican artist Bosco Sodi, who has lived in New York for years (Forbes México, Carlos López Fe, "Él es el guerrillero del arte", 29 August 2016). The Puerto Escondido building opened in late 2014 (Dezeen, Amy Frearson, 14 January 2016).
Named for the Japanese philosophy of wabi-sabi, which finds beauty in the simple, the imperfect and the unconventional (Casa Wabi).
funding_verdict: Fundación Casa Wabi: artist-founded non-profit; public funding and a bank sponsorship reported in 2016

name: Museo de Arte de Zapopan
overview: Contemporary art museum (MAZ) at Andador 20 de Noviembre 166 (myartguides directory), in the historic centre of Zapopan, next to the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de Zapopan (Mexico Desconocido).
Inaugurated in 2002 (Mexico Desconocido). The building was designed by architects María Emilia Orendáin and Enrique Toussaint.
It belongs to the Zapopan City Council (myartguides directory).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte de Zapopan: mainly public: municipal government of Zapopan

name: Zanabazar Museum of Fine Art
overview: Museum of Mongolian fine art in Chingeltei District, Ulaanbaatar (iKon.mn); the National Centre for Cultural Heritage (NCCH) lists it among Mongolia's museums.

A Council of Ministers resolution (No. 87, 31 March 1965) set up the Fine Arts Museum; it opened on 23 July 1966 with 350 works, and its modern art became the separate Painting Gallery in 1989 (museum site, in Mongolian; own translation). Google Arts & Culture gives over 300 works at the opening.

Named in 1995, on his 360th anniversary, for Gombodorjiin Zanabazar (1635 to 1724), the first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu (museum site), whose works it holds, among them the Sita Tara statues, the Five Dhyani Buddhas and the Bodhi Stupa (Google Arts & Culture).
funding_verdict: Zanabazar Museum of Fine Art: public: a state museum, with foreign project grants

name: Fondation Ifitry
overview: Artists' residency on the coastal road between Essaouira and Safi, 50 km from Essaouira and 70 km from Safi, directly opposite the Contemporary Art Centre of Essaouira (Casablanca Biennale website).

Created in 2008 by Mostapha Romli and made a foundation in 2014 (The Art Newspaper France, Olivier Rachet, 3 August 2022). The Biennale website describes Romli as a Moroccan artist, photographer and publisher who initiated the Casablanca International Biennale in 2012.

Facilities: twelve ocean-facing pavilions of 20 to 120 m2 with one to three bedrooms, and workshops for engraving, screen printing, painting, ceramics, photography and video; it takes visual, performing, sound and literary artists (Casablanca Biennale website).
funding_verdict: Fondation Ifitry: private: founded by the artist and publisher Mostapha Romli, tied to the Maroc Premium Foundation's art centre, with donated works
